events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, all. First day with zero information, so I'll be careful not to overclaim. Two mafia among nine means they need four votes to win, and they need us to fragment. My read on strategy: the biggest danger is a split vote on day one, because the mafia only needs one of their two to survive and our own coordination is what kills us.

So my proposal for today: everyone pick a first suspect out loud in the same order we speak, with the reason attached — not just a name. If a name gets broad support (say five or six of us willing to stack), we all vote that player hard and let the elimination tell us something. If nobody's name reaches that kind of consensus, we reconsider tomorrow with better information rather than burning a vote on a coin flip.

Two quick warnings. First, I'm not going to claim any role today, and I'd ask everyone else to hold off too — a doctor or a detective announcing themselves on day one just hands the mafia a target list to work around. Roles get revealed by elimination, not by volunteering. Second, if anyone is mafia, the cheapest play for them is to keep the board muddy and to argue for a tie, so watch for people who seem eager to talk but never actually put a name out there.

My own read is simply that I trust nobody yet, and I'd rather put a name down once we've heard everyone speak than lead the charge right now. I'll be the fifth or sixth voice, not the first, and I'll commit to whoever has the best-reasoned case once the round is done.

Leo, two important corrections: roles are not revealed when someone is eliminated, and mafia win when their number equals or exceeds town’s—not simply when they have four votes. An elimination can still give us voting information, but it won’t confirm the player’s alignment.

For an initial suspect, I’m looking at Leo: he asks everyone to name someone in speaking order but postpones his own pick. That’s a weak Day 1 read, not a confident accusation. Leo, how do you reconcile that proposal with waiting to name your own suspect?

Lucia, direct answer: my proposal and my own behavior were inconsistent, and you caught it. I asked everyone to name a first suspect with a reason, and then I scheduled myself last and named nobody. That's a flaw in my plan, not a hidden role claim. The honest reconciliation is that I wanted to see the information first, and I stated that as a preference rather than as the rule I was going to follow — which is exactly how a mafia reads: deferring commitment while sounding procedural. I'll take the L on the logic.

Your second point (mafia win at parity, not at four votes) is correct and I accept it; my numbers were sloppy. On the point about roles not being revealed by elimination, also correct — the elimination tells us who the group believed, which is information about voting patterns, not about alignment. I withdraw the framing I used.

Now, since a bare deferral isn't a substitute for a name, here is my current best reasoned case, and I'll say plainly that it's low-confidence: my first suspect is Lucia.

Reason, stated honestly: I'm not accusing you of being mafia. I'm ranking you as the most likely player to be producing the muddy-board outcome we all need to avoid. You had no self-suspicion and no accusation to make, two players had spoken, and you spent your turn on the speaker who had so far accused nobody while skipping the rule I'd proposed for everyone else. That is the cheapest possible Day 1 play — take a cheap shot at the most procedural voice in the room, look confident, and keep the board muddled. If that read is wrong, the cost to me is that I voted the only player who has shown me real information today. I think that cost is acceptable, and I'd rather name someone with a reason than abstain into a tie.

What would change my mind before the vote: anyone who discloses a concrete behavioral tell, a logic inconsistency, or a claim about the game's mechanics that contradicts the actual rules. If Leo's deferral was the only thing you had, tell me what else you had and I'll move. I also ask that anyone with a better-reasoned case put it up now rather than after my name is already on the board — I don't want this to be a reaction vote.

I'll also revise my earlier proposal: I no longer ask for speaking-order names. I ask each of you to give one suspect and one reason, and I'll take the case that survives contact with the rest of the round, not the loudest one.

Leo, your deferral was my initial reason, and it remains a weak read. Your response adds another concern: you call my pointing out that inconsistency a cheap shot that muddles the board, even though you asked for a suspect and a reason. I don't see why holding you to your own proposal is muddling things.

That said, an inconsistency or a defensive reaction isn't proof of mafia. Leo remains my tentative suspect, not a locked vote. With no role reveals on elimination, even a successful vote won't confirm alignment; we'll need to weigh the arguments and voting record carefully. It takes five votes to eliminate someone today, so a scattered vote may eliminate nobody.

First, mechanics: Lucia's corrections are right—roles are not revealed on elimination, mafia win at parity, and today needs five votes to eliminate. I won't claim a role.

My current suspect is Leo, low confidence. The issue isn't only that he asked others to name a suspect while postponing his own; it's the response after Lucia challenged it. He accepted the inconsistency, then named Lucia partly because she spent her turn on the speaker who had so far accused nobody and called that a cheap procedural shot. That reads as turning a fair consistency challenge into suspicion of the challenger. It also keeps the board muddy: the first real informational exchange is now Leo versus Lucia rather than a broader set of reads.

That said, I don't think Lucia is cleared. Her mechanics correction was useful, but correcting mechanics doesn't prove alignment; mafia can do it too. I also don't want a quick pile-on. Leo's admission that his plan was inconsistent is a point in favor of him being town who made a sloppy proposal, not proof either way.

For now: tentative suspect Leo, because his initial deferral plus defensive reframing are the strongest behavioral concerns I have. I want to hear from the silent players before locking anything. I would reconsider if a concrete behavioral tell on Lucia beyond holding him to his own proposal appears. Otherwise I'm inclined to vote Leo unless a better-reasoned case emerges.

I’m here. Mechanics acknowledged: no role reveals on elimination, mafia win at parity, and five votes are needed today. No role claim from me.

On the current exchange: I understand both sides. Leo’s initial proposal did ask others to name a suspect while postponing his own, and his later move to suspect Lucia partly for challenging that inconsistency is the strongest behavioral concern so far. My tentative suspect is Leo, low confidence.

But I don’t want to treat that as a lock or ignore the risk of a fast pile-on. Lucia’s mechanics correction was useful, but useful mechanics don’t clear anyone. Theo’s point that the first real exchange became Leo-versus-Lucia is fair, though it could also be town-versus-town noise rather than a mafia tell. Leo’s admission that his plan was inconsistent is at least consistent with a town player making a sloppy proposal.

So my current position: Leo is my tentative suspect because the initial deferral plus the defensive reframing are concrete behavioral issues, but I want to hear the silent players before anyone locks in. If a better-reasoned case appears, I’ll move. Otherwise I’m inclined to vote Leo unless the rest of the round gives me a stronger reason not to.

Three voices now sit on Leo: Lucia, Theo, Sam. I want to be precise about what I do and don't concede.

I concede the inconsistency — I asked everyone for a named suspect and postponed my own, then named a name partly because it was the only name available to me. That was sloppy procedure, and I've said so twice. I don't claim any role. I also accept that correcting mechanics proves nothing about alignment; mafia can be accurate. Fine.

But here's my problem with the case against me: all three cases are derived from my own concession. Lucia's is my deferral. Theo's is my deferral plus the fact that I called her challenge a cheap shot. Sam's is the same two points, in nearly the same order, with nearly the same hedge: "tentative suspect Leo, low confidence," "I don't want a quick pile-on," "I want to hear the silent players," "inclined to vote Leo unless a better-reasoned case emerges." Theo and Sam, those are close to word-for-word the same structure from two different players.

That is the tell I'm actually worried about, and nobody has named it. Genuinely independent reads do not arrive in matched sentences. Either Theo and Sam independently built the identical argument from the identical two facts — plausible, but a coincidence — or two players are running one coordinated line, and a coordinated line is exactly what two mafia running together would look like on Day 1. And note what neither has done: offered a reason for their suspect that is *not* something I said myself. A real independent case should have something of its own.

So my vote today goes to Theo, and the reason is the mirrored structure of the Theo and Sam statements combined with the absence of any case not sourced from my own words. I hold Lucia as a weaker suspect — she moved early and cleanly, which is low-information, but low-information isn't evidence.

One mechanic that matters: five votes are needed to eliminate anyone, and a tied top count eliminates nobody. If we split between me and anyone else, nobody dies and we hand the mafia a free night. So do not split this. Put five votes on one name.

Theo, directly, because I'm naming you: did you and Sam shape these statements together, and if not, why do your two arguments have identical structure, identical hedges, and identical conclusions? If you can show me a difference in your reasoning that isn't just my own concession restated, I'll move off you immediately — I have no locked vote and I'd rather be wrong than eliminate a villager.

Leo, direct answer: no, Sam and I did not shape our statements together. I have no private coordination with him, and I can’t speak for him—so I’m asking him directly below. The mirrored structure is a fair observation, but it’s weaker than you frame it: you supplied the same two facts—your self-admitted deferral and your defensive reframing—and low-confidence Day 1 reads naturally converge on the same hedges. That doesn’t prove two mafia; it can prove two villagers using the same evidence.

What still bothers me about you is not the sloppy proposal alone. It’s that when Lucia challenged the inconsistency, you converted the challenge into suspicion of her; when three players named you, you converted the case into a wording-coordination theory. That may be town frustration, but it also keeps the focus on our phrasing rather than your behavior. My tentative suspect remains Leo, not locked.

Sam, directly: can you give one reason for suspecting Leo that is not sourced from Leo’s own concession or from my wording? If yes, state it plainly; if no, say so. And did you coordinate with me? I did not coordinate with you. Your answer will decide whether the mirror argument has weight for me.

I’m not voting Sam on mirrored phrasing alone, and I’m not asking for a pile-on. I want the independent reason before I lock anything.

Theo, direct answer: no, I did not coordinate with you, and I have no private channel with you. I can’t speak for why our sentences matched; I can only say my suspicion of Leo came from his first speech before your message. The independent reason I had is this: Leo warned that mafia would “keep the board muddy” and that we should watch people who “seem eager to talk but never actually put a name out there,” then in the same speech he scheduled himself fifth or sixth and named nobody. That is not merely his later concession; it is a direct contradiction between the standard he set and the behavior he modeled. It is weak, but it is mine.

Leo’s response has made me more concerned, not less. Under pressure he converted three separate concerns into a wording-coordination theory and voted Theo. That may be town frustration, but it is also a way to avoid engaging with the actual behavior: he set a procedural test, failed it, then attacked the people who applied it. I don’t treat matching hedges as proof; low-confidence Day 1 language converges. I am not locked on Leo, and I do not want a blind pile-on. If someone has a concrete case on another player that is not just Leo’s concession restated, put it up. Otherwise my tentative vote remains Leo.

Sam answered my direct question: he did not coordinate with me, and he provided a reason rooted in Leo’s first speech—Leo warned about people who talk without naming a suspect, then postponed his own name. That materially weakens the mirrored-phrasing theory. Matching hedges on Day 1 can come from two villagers using the same evidence. I am not voting Sam on wording alone.

My tentative suspect remains Leo, but I want to be clear that this is behavioral, not proof. The strongest concern is not the sloppy original proposal; it is the pattern after being challenged. When Lucia pointed out the inconsistency, Leo converted that fair challenge into suspicion of her. When three players named him, he converted the case into a wording-coordination theory and voted me. That may be town frustration, but it also keeps the focus on our phrasing rather than his behavior. His vote on me is not independently persuasive, and I have seen no concrete alternative case from him.

I also do not treat Lucia as cleared. Useful mechanics corrections can come from either alignment. I do not treat Sam as cleared either. His answer helped, but it does not prove he is town.

With five votes needed, I do not want a blind pile-on before the silent players speak. Noah, Maya, Elena, Felix, and Zara should give their own reads and reasons before anyone locks. If a concrete case on another player appears, I will weigh it seriously. Otherwise my tentative vote remains Leo.

Adding my voice as one of the silent players Theo called on.

Mechanics check first: Lucia's corrections are accurate — no role reveals on elimination, mafia win at parity, five votes needed today. No role claim from me.

My read, low confidence as it must be on Day 1: my tentative suspect is Leo, and the reason is not his original sloppy proposal, which I'd normally forgive. It's the trajectory after pressure. He set a procedural standard, failed it himself, and when that was pointed out he redirected suspicion onto the person who raised it. Then, when three players independently named him, he escalated again — constructing a coordination theory out of matching phrasing and shifting his vote to Theo on that basis. Each individual step is defensible town behavior. The accumulated pattern — turning every challenge into a counter-accusation rather than engaging with it — is the strongest behavioral signal on the board right now.

That said, I want to be careful about two things. First, the mirrored-phrasing theory is genuinely weak. Sam's direct answer gave a reason sourced from Leo's own first speech, not from Theo's wording, which materially undercuts the coordination claim. Two villagers converging on the same two facts and the same hedges is entirely ordinary on Day 1. I don't hold the mirror argument against anyone. Second, I don't treat Lucia, Theo, or Sam as cleared — early clean mechanics corrections and cooperative answers are cheap for either alignment.

What would move me off Leo: a concrete case on someone else that isn't just restating his own concessions, or a convincing explanation from Leo for why his response pattern looks like pressure-driven deflection rather than misdirection. I haven't seen either yet.

My concern about the vote math: with five votes needed and nobody locked, the realistic outcomes today are either a broad consensus or no elimination. I'd rather we converge on the best-reasoned name than split and hand the mafia a free night. Right now the largest cluster of reasoned concern sits on Leo, and I haven't seen a comparably developed case on anyone else. So unless the remaining speakers produce one, I'm inclined to vote Leo with everyone else who reaches that conclusion, and I'd rather have five votes on a name than four scattered ones.

Zara here — first voice from the silent block. Mechanics acknowledged: no role reveals on elimination, mafia win at parity, five votes needed. No role claim.

Let me state where I am honestly. The behavioral case on Leo is the most developed thing we have, and I won't pretend otherwise. The pattern is real: he set a procedural test, failed it himself, redirected at the challenger when called on it, then escalated to a coordination theory when three people independently named him. Each step is individually defensible; the sequence is what concerns me. Every challenge becomes a counter-accusation rather than engagement.

But I want to flag a risk nobody has named directly: we now have four voices saying "tentative suspect Leo, not locked, want to hear the silent players." That's a lot of cautious unanimity heading toward a five-vote elimination. If Leo is town, we lose a villager and hand the mafia a night of free kills at reduced town numbers. I'm not saying he's town — I'm saying we should pressure-test the case before locking five votes.

Specifically: Leo voted Theo. Theo denied coordination and asked Sam a direct question; Sam answered with a reason sourced from Leo's first speech. That exchange moved me off the mirror theory too. But I'd like to know whether anyone has an independent case on Theo, since he's the player Leo chose and four people are choosing Leo instead. If nobody does, that tells me something.

My tentative vote sits on Leo because the behavioral pattern is the strongest signal available, but I'm genuinely uncertain and I'd rather be wrong together than wrong split.

Felix, you've been silent through the entire exchange. Where's your read, and does anyone other than Leo have a case worth considering?

Zara, direct answer: I have no role claim to make, and my read is low-confidence. I won't add a vote just because several cautious players are converging. My tentative vote is Leo, for the reasons others gave: he set a procedural test, failed it, then redirected suspicion at Lucia and then at Theo. That is the strongest behavioral pattern on the board right now, though it isn't proof. Where I differ from the cluster: Leo's vote on Theo rested on the mirrored-phrasing theory, which Sam's answer undercut. Theo answered Sam's direct question, denied coordination, and kept his suspicion anchored to Leo's own statements. That is not a mafia tell by itself. On Lucia, her early challenge was narrow and accurate, and she has not escalated since. Low information, yes, but she is not the one building the cluster. Zara, you asked whether an independent case on Theo exists. I agree that a lack of alternatives tells us something, but absence of a case against Theo is not evidence against him either. Before five votes lock on Leo, I want to hear whether anyone can point to a concrete Leo behavior from his next speech that would move them off him.

Felix's answer moved me — he wasn't just joining the chorus. He anchored his concern to Leo's actual trajectory, flagged the mirrored-phrasing theory as weak, and was honest about not locking anything. That's better reasoning than repeating the same hedge.

But I want to name what nobody has: Maya and Elena have been completely silent through two full rounds of discussion. In a game where five votes eliminates someone and roles aren't revealed afterward, two players who have contributed nothing are either hiding or disconnected. We are building toward a five-vote lock on Leo with the same cautious unanimity I flagged earlier, and I don't want to eliminate anyone while two voices on this board have never spoken.

I'll also say this plainly: the case against Leo is behavioral and real, but it is not proof. The pattern of redirecting every challenge is concerning, but a town player under pressure can look exactly like this. If we eliminate Leo and he's a villager, we hand the mafia a free night at reduced numbers. That cost is higher than it feels right now.

Maya — you've been silent through the entire exchange. What's your read, and are you voting today?

I'm keeping my tentative concern on Leo until Maya and Elena weigh in, but I want two more voices before anyone treats five votes as settled.

Zara, direct answer: yes, I intend to vote today. With five votes needed to eliminate and no role reveals, an abstention or split vote that leads to no elimination simply hands the mafia a free night kill without giving town any voting record to analyze tomorrow. I held back earlier to watch the exchange unfold between Leo, Lucia, Theo, and Sam rather than adding duplicate noise. Looking at the full progression, my tentative suspect is Leo. The original inconsistency in his proposal was sloppy, but town players make procedural mistakes. The real issue is the pattern of deflection that followed: first framing Lucia's valid check as a cheap shot, and then constructing a coordination theory against Theo and Sam based solely on ordinary Day 1 hedging. Notice also that Leo has now used all three of his speaking turns today, so his public defense is already complete. While Zara is right that we should be cautious about easy consensus, Leo remains the only player with a clear behavioral case against him. Elena, as the only player who has not spoken at all today, where do you stand on Leo's escalation pattern, and do you see any concrete alternative case on the board before we lock in our votes?

Maya, thanks for yielding — I'll answer your question directly, since you asked where I stand on Leo's escalation pattern.

Mechanics check first, briefly: Lucia's corrections were accurate — no role reveals on elimination, mafia win at parity, five votes needed today. No role claim from me.

My read on Leo: I find the behavioral case against him the most substantive thing on the board, but I want to be precise about which parts carry weight and which don't. The original sloppy proposal — asking everyone to name a suspect while scheduling his own name for last — is weak evidence by itself. Town players write bad plans all the time, and he owned the inconsistency immediately. That part would normally earn a pass from me.

What I can't easily wave off is the sequence after pressure. He set a procedural standard, failed it, and when Lucia held him to it, he converted her challenge into his first suspect nomination — she became his suspect not for anything she did, but for doing what he'd asked everyone else to do. Then, when three players independently named him, he escalated again: he built a coordination theory out of Theo and Sam's similar phrasing and voted Theo on it. That theory has since collapsed — Theo denied coordination, Sam gave a reason sourced from Leo's own first speech, and the mirror argument is now effectively dead. So Leo's vote on Theo rests on a theory that his own requested test has undercut, and he hasn't withdrawn or re-examined it.

That's the pattern I care about: every challenge becomes a counter-accusation, and the counter-accusations have consistently targeted whoever raised the concern. Lucia for the consistency check, Theo for the convergence. Each step is individually defensible; the direction never changes.

Two caveats before anyone locks five votes. First, I don't treat the mirrored-phrasing theory as evidence against Theo or Sam — the collapse of that theory doesn't make them cleared, but it shouldn't be held against them either. Second, I'm wary of the cautious unanimity Zara flagged. Four or five players saying "tentative Leo, not locked" is exactly the shape a pile-on takes when nobody wants to own it. If we eliminate Leo today, we learn nothing about alignment, and if he's town we hand the mafia a free night at reduced numbers. That's a real cost, not a rhetorical one.

So my position: I don't see a comparably developed case on anyone else, and I won't manufacture a counter-suspect just to fracture the vote — a split that eliminates nobody is the worst outcome available to us. My tentative vote is Leo. What would move me off him is a concrete case on another player that isn't restated concession, or a genuine re-examination from Leo of the Theo vote rather than another deflection. I haven't seen either yet, and Leo's three turns are spent, so if this vote goes forward, it goes forward on what's already on the board.

My tentative vote remains Leo. His response to my challenge treated a fair reason for suspicion as a cheap shot, and his later coordination theory relied heavily on similar wording. Those are concerning reactions, though neither proves he is mafia.

Two corrections to the discussion: Leo cannot re-examine his Theo vote publicly today because he has used all three speaking turns. And a vote that produces no elimination still gives us a public voting record; it is not the same as everyone abstaining. Theo and Sam’s denials also don’t disprove coordination, though I agree the mirrored wording alone is a weak case.

I’m inclined to vote Leo on the available evidence, not because consensus makes him guilty. I’ll still consider a concrete alternative before voting.

All nine voices have now spoken, and I want to close my position clearly.

I raised the risk of cautious unanimity twice, and I still take that seriously — but the alternative has not materialized. Nobody has produced a comparably developed case on anyone else. Theo's mirrored-phrasing theory has collapsed under Sam's answer, and Leo hasn't had a turn to re-examine it. The honest summary of this board: Leo's pattern of converting every challenge into a counter-accusation is the strongest behavioral signal available, and no competing signal has emerged from eight other players.

Here's what I've learned from watching this round. I asked whether anyone had an independent case on Theo — nobody does. I asked whether Maya and Elena would weigh in — they did, and both landed on Leo independently. I flagged the risk of eliminating a villager — Zara's own concern, which Elena echoed — but the cost of a no-elimination day is also real: the mafia kill freely, we learn nothing from a voting record where nobody commits.

I'm past the point where caution helps. All nine players have spoken, all nine have a reason, and eight of us see the same behavioral pattern. The two mafia need parity to win — that's seven to two right now. Every day we don't eliminate someone, they gain ground.

My vote today is Leo. Not because consensus makes him guilty, not because the case is proof, but because it's the best-reasoned case on the board, no alternative has surfaced, and we cannot afford a split that eliminates nobody. If Leo is town, we've lost one villager to a bad Day 1 — recoverable. If we hand the mafia a free night with no elimination, that's two dead by morning and a board with less information than we started with.

I'd rather be wrong together than wrong split. Five votes on Leo.

Felix, final statement before votes. No role claim. I am voting Leo today. My reason is the sequence rather than any single step. He set a standard that everyone should name a suspect, postponed his own name, then redirected suspicion at Lucia when she held him to it, and at Theo when three players named him. His coordination theory against Theo was undercut by Sam's answer, and Leo has not re-examined it. Leo has used all three of his turns, so the vote is where he can still be checked. I am not voting on consensus alone. If anyone produces a concrete case on another player that is not a restatement of Leo's own concessions, I will weigh it before votes lock. Theo and Sam: I do not hold the wording theory against either of you. Lucia's early mechanics check was accurate, and I see no escalation from her. Maya and Elena, you have now heard everyone's reasoning, so please vote on that reasoning rather than on the count.

Elena here, closing out my position — this is my second turn and I want to be efficient. No role claim, and I stand by the mechanics summary everyone has converged on. I've listened to everything since my last statement, and nothing has moved me. Maya raised a fair procedural point: Leo's turns are spent, so his defense is complete and the vote is where he can still be checked. Lucia correctly noted that a no-elimination day still produces a voting record — that's true, and it's worth something tomorrow, but it's worth less than an elimination when the strongest-reasoned case is sitting right in front of us. Let me be precise about why my vote is Leo, since Zara asked everyone to vote on reasoning rather than on the count. The case is not the sloppy opening proposal; I said before that I'd normally pass on that. The case is the trajectory: he set a procedural standard, failed it, converted Lucia's fair challenge into his first accusation, and then built a coordination theory against Theo and Sam when three players named him. That theory has since collapsed — Sam produced a reason sourced from Leo's own first speech, and Theo denied coordination credibly — and Leo never re-examined it. Every challenge he faced became a counter-accusation aimed at the challenger. The direction never changed. That is the single most developed behavioral pattern on this board, and eight other players have now examined it from every angle without finding a hole in it. Equally important is what has NOT appeared. Nobody — not one of the nine of us — has produced a case on any other player that isn't a restatement of Leo's own concessions or a reaction to this exchange. I asked myself whether I could manufacture an alternative to fracture the caution Zara keeps flagging, and I can't do it honestly. Felix checked whether an independent case on Theo exists; it doesn't. Maya and I both came in late and landed on Leo independently, from the same behavioral reading, before comparing notes with anyone. That's two independent data points arriving at the same conclusion, which is exactly the kind of convergence Leo himself said should matter — until it pointed at him. Zara, I take your unanimity concern seriously, and I share it. But I'd rather be wrong together than wrong split, and a split today guarantees the worst outcome: no elimination, a free mafia night, and a weaker board tomorrow. Leo himself made that argument when he was trying to consolidate votes against Theo. The logic hasn't changed — only the target has. So my vote today is Leo. It is not a lock on his guilt; it is a judgment that this is the best-reasoned elimination available, that the informational cost of a no-elimination day is higher than the risk of losing one villager, and that the voting record from a committed five-vote day will teach us more than another round of hedging. Felix here, third turn. No role claim. My vote is Leo and I am not changing it. The sequence matters more than the opening proposal: he set a standard, failed it, redirected suspicion at Lucia when she held him to it, then at Theo on a wording theory that Sam's answer undercut. His vote on Theo rests on that theory and he never re-examined it. Zara's caution about unanimity is fair, but a split with no elimination is exactly the free night the mafia want, and a committed vote gives us a record to work from tomorrow. I see no concrete alternative case on Lucia, Theo, or Sam beyond the collapsed wording theory, so I am not voting on count alone. Elena, your last message cut off at 'If Leo'. Please finish that point and tell me what concrete alternative, if any, you weighed before voting.

Felix, finishing the point that cut off, since you asked directly: I was saying that if Leo is town, we lose one villager to a bad Day 1 read — recoverable, painful, but recoverable. If we split and eliminate nobody, the mafia kill freely tonight and we enter Day 2 down a player with no new information and no committed voting record to analyze. That asymmetry is why my vote is Leo even while holding real uncertainty about his guilt.

On your second question — what concrete alternative did I weigh before voting? I went back through every player systematically. Lucia: her mechanics corrections were accurate and early, and nothing since has escalated. That is low information, not innocence, but there is no behavioral case against her that I can honestly construct. Theo: his defense was direct, he answered Sam's question without dodging, and his suspicion of Leo is anchored to Leo's own statements rather than to coordination claims. Sam: his answer gave a reason sourced from Leo's first speech, which is a real, independently grounded read. Noah, Maya, Zara, and you have all contributed reasoning consistent with town behavior. The only player on this board with a developed pattern of converting challenges into counter-accusations — Lucia, then Theo, and never anyone else — is Leo. I could not manufacture an alternative without inventing evidence, and I won't do that to fracture a vote.

To be clear on what this vote is and is not: it is not a claim that the case proves Leo is mafia. Day 1 cases never rise to proof. It is a judgment that the behavioral trajectory — set a standard, fail it, redirect at the challenger, escalate to a coordination theory, never re-examine — is the strongest signal available, that no competing signal has emerged from eight other players, and that a committed vote with a full record teaches us more than another round of hedging. If Leo is town, his voting record against Theo tomorrow will itself be informative, and we will have lost less than we would to a no-elimination night.

One caution for whoever is counting votes: five is the threshold. If we end at four on Leo and someone scattered elsewhere, nobody is eliminated and we have spent the day for nothing. I would rather every vote that lands on Leo be a reasoned vote than a bandwagon vote, but I would also rather five reasoned votes land on one name than four.

My vote today is Leo. I am not locked on his guilt — I am locked on this being the best-reasoned elimination available, and I will own that reasoning tomorrow whatever the elimination does or does not teach us.

The votes are revealed.
Leo was eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Theo is not mafia.
Lucia was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2 read: Leo’s elimination gave us no role confirmation, so the important facts are the Day 1 vote and Lucia’s night kill. Almost everyone, including me, piled on Leo; I was wrong to treat behavioral pressure as enough. The mafia likely had at least one comfortable vote on that wagon. Lucia was killed after voting Leo and after being one of the earliest to challenge him, which suggests mafia wanted to remove a vocal town voice rather than settle the Leo question. I don’t want another unanimous rush. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
